Partly documented, partly the “enforced” half is more Zamyatin’s satire than history. Spoiler-free, since you’re mid-book.

What’s documented: the early Soviet state did radically liberalize sex and family law. The 1918 Family Code made marriage civil, made divorce easy, and erased the legal distinction for illegitimate children. Abortion was legalized in 1920, and the 1922 criminal code dropped the tsarist ban on homosexuality. Alexandra Kollontai was the big theorist, arguing for “winged Eros,” free unions, and moving child-rearing and housework out of the private household. The “glass of water” idea (sex should be as casual as drinking water) was also circulating.

Where “encouraged” overstates it: the leadership was mostly prudish. Clara Zetkin’s recollection of Lenin has him calling the glass-of-water theory un-Marxist, though her account was written down later. By 1924 Aron Zalkind was publishing sexual “commandments” for the revolutionary proletariat that preached restraint, and by the 1930s the regime swung back to traditional family values. Kollontai’s most famous essays also came after Zamyatin wrote We (1920-21).

The “enforced” part: there was a famous 1918 “decree on the socialization of women,” supposedly from anarchists in Saratov or Vladimir. It’s generally treated as a hoax or propaganda, but it was widely believed and circulated, especially by anti-Bolshevik press. Zamyatin was writing right in that rumor-soaked environment.

What scholars generally argue: the Lex Sexualis (each number has a right to any other number) is aimed less at Bolshevik policy than at a lineage of utopian sex-communism, from Plato’s Republic through Fourier to Chernyshevsky’s What Is to Be Done?. Zamyatin spent 1916-17 in England as a shipbuilding engineer and was steeped in Taylorism, so the real target is the rationalization of everything, with sex just the most striking thing to schedule. He said the novel warns against the twin dangers of machine power and state power
